units.title: Chest wall
units.summary: Build a map of ribs, sternum and the protective thoracic cage.
units.lesson: The thoracic wall supports breathing and protects the organs beneath it. Begin at the manubrium, follow the body of the sternum and find its xiphoid process. Compare the first ribs with the lower ribs. Costal cartilage connects the anterior rib ends to the sternum in different patterns. Intercostal nerves and vessels need special attention when opening the chest wall. The removable model is a teaching aid; it does not represent a clinical incision plan.

units.title: Pleura & lungs
units.summary: Explore lung lobes, pleural layers and the diaphragm.
units.lesson: The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two. Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the thoracic cavity. The pleural space is normally a potential space between those surfaces. The diaphragm forms the floor of the thorax. Keep anatomical left and right anchored to the specimen, not your screen.

units.title: Airways
units.summary: Follow the trachea into the main bronchi and lobar branches.
units.lesson: Air passes from the trachea into the right and left main bronchi and then into branching airways. Trace each route in three dimensions. Cavity reference regions in this collection represent spaces, not pieces of myocardium.

units.title: Pneumothorax
units.summary: A breathless adult has a right pneumothorax. The case team has selected a small-bore chest drain.
units.lesson: Air separates the right lung from its chest wall. Review the chest X-ray and the agreed drainage site. Work through a small-bore, wire-guided drain sequence on the enlarged chest-wall model. Its skin, rib, intercostal bundle, pleural space and lung show what each instrument must preserve.

units.title: Aortic valve stenosis
units.summary: A heart team has selected transfemoral TAVI for severe aortic stenosis in a fictional adult.
units.lesson: The replacement travels through a femoral artery and the aorta to the native valve. It expands inside that valve rather than removing it. Follow the enlarged vessel model, position the replacement, then check function, coronary openings and the access site.
units.response: The replacement opens within the native valve. Continue rhythm, valve and groin-site monitoring; watch for leakage, bleeding, stroke symptoms and conduction problems.
units.limitations: Fictional, fixed-indication learning scenario. Responses are illustrative and time-compressed. The model does not establish clinical competence or predict a real patient outcome.
